incidents.name: EFLeverVault flash-loan balance inflation
incidents.notes: EFLeverVault priced shares off its own ETH balance and exposed an unguarded receiveFlashLoan() callback, so anyone could have Balancer flash-loan WETH into the vault and then withdraw far more ETH than they had deposited.

sources.ref: onchain review: EFLeverVault 0xe39fd820b58f83205db1d9225f28105971c3d309 created 2022-05-27T05:12:32Z by 0xbf58e21b232ceea012122dd1fd60daad5791aa2e, unrelated to the attack sender; plain contract, no EIP-1967 events, age from deployment. The recorded tx is the generalised front-runner 0x26bce6ec... that landed first and took the ~750 ETH; the original exploiter 0xdf31F4C8dC9548eb4c416Af26dC396A25FDE4D5F ran the same call in 0x160c5950a01b88953648ba90ec0a29b0c5383e055d35a7835d905c53a3dda01e in the same block. 750 ETH x $1,325.14 at incidentTimestamp 1665748727 (DefiLlama) = $993,853.

re-check 2026 (deployment-basis rows with a DELEGATECALL in the runtime): CONFIRMED deployment basis. The vault's runtime is byte-identical at the creation block 14852275 and the incident block 15746200, and its 61 DELEGATECALL sites are solc external-library calls to the link-time SafeMath at 0x071108ad85d7a766b41e0f5e5195537a8fc8e74d (the address Etherscan reports as the linked library; its runtime begins 73<self>3014 and is constant across the window). callTracer on the exploit tx confirms that library is the only delegatecall target. The vault does expose an owner-only arbitrary `to.delegatecall(data)`, which can write storage but cannot change the vault's own runtime code, so it is not an upgrade mechanism.
